title: What Skinner, Criminology, and a Year 9 Boy Taught Me About Behaviour
author: Wheadon, Richard
summary: A Year 9 student's candid explanation — that he only completes homework for teachers who actually follow through with detentions — becomes the entry point for a wide-ranging argument about what really changes behavior in schools. Richard Wheadon draws on B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning experiments and criminologist Daniel Nagin's deterrence research to make the case that predictability, not severity, is the key driver of behavioral change. Skinner's Skinner Box experiments demonstrated that consistent consequences stabilized behavior while inconsistent ones produced erratic, calculating responses — exactly the pattern students display when some teachers enforce rules and others do not. Nagin's 2013 review of deterrence studies reached the same conclusion from decades of criminology research: people change their behavior based on the certainty of consequence, not its harshness. Wheadon extends this to three everyday examples — average-speed cameras, random breath testing for drink-driving, and parking enforcement — each of which shows that behavioral change follows the perceived inevitability of being caught, not the size of the penalty. Applied to schools: when students know that a consequence will happen, behavior becomes a routine; when they're uncertain, it becomes a gamble. Individual acts of compassion by teachers who bend the rules — however well-intentioned — collectively erode the system's predictability and thereby harm the very students the compassion was meant to help.
points: Predictability of consequences is the actual driver of behavior change in schools — not the severity of punishment — a finding that holds across Skinner's animal experiments, Nagin's criminology review, and ordinary examples from speed cameras to parking enforcement.

When individual teachers make compassionate exceptions to behavior policies, collectively those exceptions erode the system's predictability, which paradoxically creates more confusion and stress for the very students the compassion was meant to support.

Skinner showed that inconsistent reinforcement produces unstable, calculating behavior — animals and students alike learn the 'real rules' of the environment: not the ones written in policy, but the ones that are actually enforced.

Certainty of detection reduces drunk driving, speeding, and illegal parking far more reliably than increasing penalty severity — the same behavioral logic applies directly to how students calculate compliance in school settings.

Closing the 'behaviour knowing-doing gap' in schools requires not just telling teachers what the policy is but explaining the evidence behind why consistency matters — otherwise, policies get shaped by individual beliefs rather than collective consistency.
quotes: 'I do it for the teachers who actually give detentions.' Not the teachers who shouted the most. Not the ones who gave dramatic speeches. Not even the ones he liked. The teachers who changed his behaviour were the ones who followed through consistently.

Once unpredictability enters the system, behaviour becomes a calculation: 'Will this teacher follow it up?' 'Can I get away with this today?' 'Does this consequence actually happen?' The issue isn't compassion. The issue is unpredictability.
Predictable consequences strengthen behaviour. Inconsistent consequences create unstable behaviour patterns. Unpredictable reinforcement leads to confusion, resistance, and erratic responses.

Countries with extremely high speeding fines (like Switzerland) do not necessarily have lower speeding rates. What does reduce speeding is the presence of average-speed cameras, because drivers know they will be caught. The fine itself is not the deterrent. The certainty of detection is.

Daniel Nagin's 2013 review of decades of deterrence studies showed that people change their behaviour when they believe a consequence is certain, not when it is harsh. Severity has surprisingly little effect unless people think the punishment will actually happen.
Consequences are not about dominance or humiliation. They are about clarity. Predictable environments create psychological safety, fairness, stability, reduced anxiety, and clearer expectations.

Compassion and consistency are not opposites. Students need both. Where schools sometimes go wrong is trying to show compassion through inconsistency. Ironically, this often creates more confusion and stress for the very students we want to support.
Students do not rise to the level of the threat; they adapt to the consistency of the system.
